entities.summary:
Apion, also known as Apion Pleistoneices or Apion Mochthos (meaning 'toilsome'), was a prominent Hellenistic grammarian, sophist, and public figure who flourished in first-century CE Egypt, dying around 45 CE. Born in the Oasis of Siwa and educated in Alexandria, Apion became renowned for his encyclopedic knowledge, rhetorical skill, and particularly for his virulent anti-Jewish polemics. His significance in world history stems not from the survival of his own extensive writings, but from their enduring refutation by the Jewish historian Josephus, whose *Contra Apionem* (Against Apion) provides the primary window into his arguments and, inadvertently, ensures his lasting notoriety.

Apion's intellectual career was rooted in the rich scholarly tradition of Alexandria, where he studied under eminent grammarians like Didymus Chalcenterus and Euphranor. He authored numerous works, including commentaries on Homer, a history of Egypt, and a treatise on Roman antiquities, none of which survive independently. His most infamous contribution, however, was his multi-volume work *Aegyptiaca* (History of Egypt), which contained extensive accusations against the Jews, alleging their foreign origin, impious practices, and disloyalty. These polemics were not merely academic; Apion actively engaged in the heated ethno-religious conflicts of Alexandria, culminating in his role as the head of an anti-Jewish embassy to Emperor Caligula in 39-40 CE, directly opposing the Jewish delegation led by Philo.
